title: Elodie and the Smile
premise: Urban explorer Marguerite Brightwater maps a tunnel network beneath the drowned quarter of Saint-Aubin that appears on no survey, drawn by a compulsion he refuses to call belief. When his sleep-recording app captures a second voice answering questions in his own cadence, he learns the tunnels are not empty — they are a mouth, and something was invited in generations ago by the town's founding families, including his own. To survive until sunrise, Marguerite must discover which of the people helping him are already wearing borrowed faces, and accept that escaping means leaving part of himself behind as payment. In the end he walks out at dawn, but the man who emerges answers to Elodie's smile now, and the tunnels have a new mapmaker.
about_author: Noor Joubert is the pen name of a former municipal archivist who spent a decade cataloguing property records for towns that no longer exist. They write horror about paperwork, place-names, and the debts communities pretend to have forgotten.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. He presents his tunnel maps to a skeptical university contact, who points out the network matches no geological record. Marguerite dismisses it as survey error, but privately he's been dreaming in cross-sections. Beat: confident rationalism with hairline cracks showing.

chapters.title: Descent for Amateurs
chapters.summary: Marguerite leads two fellow explorers, Tomas and Ines, into the tunnels through a storm grate. The passages are too regular, brickwork too old, and their compasses agree on nothing. They find a carved lintel reading WE ASKED POLITELY. Beat: wonder curdling into unease.

chapters.title: Elodie
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Deep in the tunnels they meet a woman named Elodie who claims to be a caretaker, though her clothes are decades out of date and she knows Tomas's childhood address. She asks them each one question: what would you trade to belong somewhere? Beat: charm that reads as threat.

chapters.title: Two Came Back
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Only Marguerite and Ines surface; Tomas is simply gone, and neither can account for twenty missing minutes. Police find no record of any Tomas entering the grate. Marguerite begins recording himself sleeping to prove he isn't losing time. Beat: denial hardening into obsession.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, mostly transcript. Playback reveals a second voice in his sleep recordings — calm, patient, answering questions Marguerite never asked aloud. It knows the layout of the tunnels. It calls him by a name that isn't his. Beat: the floor drops out of his skepticism.

chapters.title: What Was Invited
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines confesses her grandmother belonged to one of Saint-Aubin's founding families and left her a sealed letter: an invitation, renewed every fifty years, that someone must carry down. The current renewal date is four days away. Beat: inherited guilt surfaces.

chapters.title: Archives and Ash
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Digging through municipal records, Marguerite finds his own surname among the founding signatories — Brightwater, listed twice, once crossed out. A photograph shows Elodie unchanged across a century. Beat: personal history revealed as complicity.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Faces
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. People around them begin acting subtly wrong — the barista who repeats yesterday exactly, Marguerite's landlord greeting him with Elodie's phrasing. Ines tests a neighbor with salt and a question only the real woman could answer. The neighbor fails. Beat: paranoia becomes method.

chapters.title: Questions in the Dark
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The second voice finally speaks while he's awake, through the recording app mid-call. It offers a bargain: bring the invitation down willingly and everyone walks free; refuse and it will come up wearing whoever it likes. Beat: negotiation as trap.

chapters.title: Tomas, Home Again
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas returns — cheerful, whole, wrong. He remembers the tunnels fondly and urges Marguerite to go back. At night Marguerite watches him stand facing a wall, smiling, for hours. Beat: grief weaponized; hope revealed as lure.

chapters.title: The Drowned Quarter
chapters.summary: Marguerite and Ines's alternating POV. They map the tunnel entrances above ground and realize every founding family's house sits on a mouth. The streets themselves form the shape of something swallowed. Beat: scale reveal — the town is the organism.

chapters.title: Renewal Notice
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The sealed letter opens itself on schedule. Inside: a list of names due, Brightwater among them, and instructions written in Marguerite's own handwriting though dated 1893. Beat: fate presented as bureaucracy; dread of inevitability.

chapters.title: Salt Lines
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. They fortify Ines's apartment, testing what holds and what doesn't. The barriers work against the borrowed faces but not against memory — Marguerite starts forgetting his mother's face while remembering the tunnels perfectly. Beat: survival costing identity.

chapters.title: What Elodie Wants
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, first time. She was the first invited, the first to say yes, and has been the mouth's voice ever since, keeping it fed so it stays polite. She doesn't want worship; she wants relief, and Marguerite's doubled name might provide it. Beat: antagonist humanized without softening the stakes.

chapters.title: The Crossed-Out Name
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. He deciphers why Brightwater appears twice in the founding records: the first Brightwater went down as payment and came back up as two people — the man and the thing that learned to answer in his voice. The second voice is family. Beat: identity horror peaks.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Grate
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Tomas leads the borrowed neighbors to Ines's door, apologizing sincerely the whole time. Ines escapes through the storm grate alone, choosing the tunnels over the street. Beat: reversal — descent becomes refuge.

chapters.title: Down Again
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Marguerite follows, carrying the invitation, having decided that going willingly is the only leverage he has. The second voice walks beside him in the dark, wearing his sleep-talk cadence, asking its questions at last. Beat: grim resolve; the interview begins.

chapters.title: The Interview
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. In the heart of the network, Elodie presides as the voice puts its questions: what would you trade to belong? Marguerite answers honestly — everything except other people — and the terms shift. Sunrise is ninety minutes away. Beat: climax of negotiation, truth under pressure.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The deal closes: the mouth releases the borrowed faces and lets the town keep its surface, but it keeps one Brightwater below and sends one up. Marguerite chooses which half of himself stays. Elodie smiles — and the smile transfers. Beat: sacrifice rendered as surgery.

chapters.title: Two Came Up
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Two figures climb out of the grate at dawn: Marguerite, and something wearing Tomas convincingly now. Ines can't tell which is which, and neither, quite, can they. Beat: ambiguous rescue; tenderness laced with terror.

chapters.title: The New Mapmaker
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Weeks later, Marguerite files a complete, accurate survey of the tunnels with the university — the first ever — and feels the mouth's approval like warmth. He sleeps soundly. The recordings capture only one voice now, but it hums. Beat: uneasy peace, corrupted belonging.

chapters.title: We Asked Politely
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Ines's POV. Ines leaves Saint-Aubin but keeps the letter, adding her own line beneath the names: a promise to come back before the next renewal, so no stranger has to. On the last page, in fresh ink, someone has written thank you. Beat: quiet resolution with the debt still open.
